beats.narration: Begin by framing Thesis Structure Overview as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. The thesis document identifies a central hypothesis or key problem(s), provides a critical review of related work, and reports methods, results, and conclusions from the associated research. Consider this worked case: A student formulates a hypothesis about algorithm efficiency, reviews prior papers, describes their experimental setup, reports performance metrics, and draws conclusions. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Thesis Structure Overview
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a three-part diagram labeled 'Hypothesis', 'Review', and 'Methods/Results/Conclusions' with arrows showing sequential flow.

beats.narration: Now define Prerequisite Alignment precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. They should respect privacy. Consider this worked case: A student who finished CSCI-589: Advanced Algorithms can directly apply those foundational concepts to their thesis project. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis. Then summarize what the example demonstrates, what it does not establish, and what evidence would be needed next.
beats.title: Prerequisite Alignment
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a simple prerequisite chain: 'CSCI-589 → CSCI-590' with a checkmark indicating readiness.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Independent Study Format operates in a concrete sequence. They should honor confidentiality. Consider this worked case: Students schedule a single weekly meeting with their advisor to discuss progress, rather than attending full lecture sections. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Independent Study Format
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a calendar with one highlighted block labeled '1 Contact Hour' alongside a 'Self-Directed Research' badge.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Term Availability and make the decision criteria explicit. They should be honest and trustworthy. Consider this worked case: A student can enroll in the Fall term to complete research over the semester, or in the Summer term for a shorter, intensive cycle. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Term Availability
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a timeline with three seasonal markers (Fall, Spring, Summer) and a 'Offered' tag next to each.

beats.narration: Apply Responsible Communication Basics to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. Consider this worked case: Instead of stating 'Our method is superior,' the student writes 'Our method reduces runtime by 15% compared to Baseline X, as shown in Table 3. 'Evidence' (italic, cited, with data reference). Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Responsible Communication Basics
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison: 'Claim' (bold, unsupported) vs. 'Evidence' (italic, cited, with data reference).

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Methods Documentation, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Consider this worked case: The student includes a reproducible protocol, specifying software versions, dataset sources, and exact parameter settings. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Methods Documentation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a checklist graphic with items: 'Reproducible Protocol', 'Software Versions', 'Dataset Sources', 'Parameter Settings'.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Results Reporting Standards with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Consider this worked case: The student presents all relevant metrics, including outliers, rather than editing data to fit a preferred narrative. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Results Reporting Standards
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a bar chart with all data points visible, labeled 'Accurate Reporting', versus a cropped chart labeled 'Misleading Selection'.

beats.narration: Use Limitations and Validity to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Consider this worked case: The student explicitly states sample size constraints and environmental variables that may affect reproducibility. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Limitations and Validity
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a 'Limitations' section box with bullet points: 'Sample Size', 'Environmental Variables', 'Reproducibility Constraints'.

beats.narration: Connect Research Integrity Practices to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Consider this worked case: The student uses citation managers to track sources and paraphrases text while maintaining proper attribution. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Research Integrity Practices
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart: 'Original Idea → Cite Source → Paraphrase → Verify Attribution → Final Draft'.

beats.narration: Finish with Ethical Computing Standards as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Computing professionals should avoid harm. Consider this worked case: The student anonymizes participant data, avoids biased testing scenarios, and discloses any conflicts of interest. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis. Then summarize what the example demonstrates, what it does not establish, and what evidence would be needed next.
beats.title: Ethical Computing Standards
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display four ethical pillars: 'Honesty', 'Trustworthiness', 'Fairness', 'Privacy/Confidentiality' with icons.

claims.text: The thesis document identifies a central hypothesis or key problem(s), provides a critical review of related work, and reports methods, results, and conclusions from the associated research.

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.
sources.title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.
sources.title: ACM Publications Policies
